title: Cialdini’s six principles of influence
body_md:
## A free sample, and a small debt

At a market stall the cheese seller presses a cube of cheddar into your hand and smiles. Now buying a wedge feels less like shopping and more like manners. Nothing sinister has happened. That pull is ordinary, and it is the first of six that Robert Cialdini described: **reciprocity** (you want to return a favour), **commitment and consistency** (you stay with a choice you have already made), **social proof** (you follow what others do), **authority** (you defer to expertise), **liking** (you say yes to people you feel close to) and **scarcity** (limited things look more valuable). He now counts a seventh, “unity”, but the title of this lesson keeps the original six. Treat the list as a way to notice pressure. It is not a lie detector.

A real colleague can do you a favour, a real shop can run low on stock, and a licensed professional can know more than you do. The danger starts when the cue stands in for evidence about the **specific action** you are being asked to take. Three questions cut through it. Who benefits? What exactly am I being asked to do? Can I check the claim somewhere I chose myself? A pile of reviews, a uniform, a logo or a warm introduction answers none of them.

### How the pulls stack

Scams rarely rely on one. A stranger sends a useful little guide (reciprocity), invites you into a trial group (commitment), lets you read the members’ glowing comments (social proof) and mentions that enrolment closes tonight (scarcity). Each step makes the next one look smaller. A pleasant start still gives you no reason to hand over money, credentials or identity documents later. In a fake investment, a small test withdrawal may be allowed on purpose, to build trust; it says nothing about whether a larger deposit is safe.

**Pause when the stakes change.** Naming the tactic helps you spot it, but it does not switch your feelings off. Before you pay, share a code, install software or grant access, check the underlying claim independently and use your ordinary approval process. A real request survives that. If an offer runs out before you can check it, missing it is safer than treating the deadline as proof.

The cases below separate ordinary persuasion from an attempt to steer your decision into a payment channel nobody has verified. In the practice you choose the next move after each new cue, and you can retry any decision or replay the whole sequence.

widget_config.goal: Recognise the influence cue, then check any request with real consequences without leaning on that cue.
widget_config.today_action: Write down one question to ask before any high-stakes offer: “How can I confirm this through a contact I already trust?”
widget_config.scope: General practice for making decisions. Cialdini describes persuasion; the NCSC and FTC examples are UK and US guidance, and rules on payments and reporting differ from place to place. The people, groups and organisers in the cases are invented.

sources.title: Cialdini / Influence at Work: principles of persuasion
sources.scope: The author’s current account of the original six principles and the seventh added later, unity.

sources.title: UK NCSC: how to spot a scam message or call
sources.scope: UK public guidance, published 2021 and reviewed 2022. It lists warning cues and independent contact, and it is not a diagnostic test.

sources.title: US FTC: How to Avoid a Scam
sources.scope: US consumer guidance (2023) on impersonation, pressure, payment methods and contacting the real organisation yourself.

sources.title: SEC and partners: relationship investment scams
sources.scope: Joint US investor alert (10 September 2024). Small early withdrawals may be allowed to create false confidence.

blocks.title: The helpful club organiser
blocks.situation: A new organiser of an online club sends you a free checklist, writes that you are exactly the kind of person the group needs, and adds you to a private chat full of glowing testimonials. Then comes the announcement: every member must pay a “verification deposit” before midnight.
blocks.analysis: The checklist and the compliments work on reciprocity and liking, the testimonials on social proof, the deadline on scarcity. None of it shows who receives the deposit or whether it is ever returned. Do not pay because the group asks. Check the organiser and the payment route independently before any money moves.

blocks.title: A genuinely limited workshop
blocks.situation: A community library lists twelve seats for a free workshop in its own published calendar. A librarian you already know mentions that booking closes once the seats are gone.
blocks.analysis: Scarcity can be real. Look at the library’s calendar, or ring the desk number it publishes. If the event is listed and booking runs through the library’s own system, the limited seats alone are no reason to turn it down. You are still free to decline, and nobody is hurrying you.

blocks.title: The invitation ladder
blocks.setup: An invented hobby forum. One of its members sends you a handy design template and invites you to a “verified makers circle”. No real account or payment is involved.

steps.prompt: You have barely looked at the group when they ask you to post a public thank-you on its page. What do you do?

choices.text: Post it at once: a gift deserves a public thank-you.
choices.consequence: Your post becomes a visible commitment, and you may feel bound to defend it.
choices.explanation: The urge to repay is only a feeling; it creates no debt. You can thank them privately without vouching for a group you have not looked at.

choices.text: Thank them for the template, and hold off recommending the group until you know it.
choices.consequence: Your gratitude stays separate from any endorsement.
choices.explanation: You are courteous to the person and withhold a public signal that others might read as a recommendation.

steps.prompt: The group’s page is full of glowing member quotes and carries a “verified by experts” badge. What next?

choices.text: Look for the organiser and the terms in a source outside that page.
choices.consequence: You get a check that the invitation itself cannot give.
choices.explanation: Find the organisation’s long-standing contact details and its written terms. If nothing confirms them, wait.

choices.text: Take the quotes and the badge as proof that the group is sound.
choices.consequence: You mistake the staging for independent evidence.
choices.explanation: A seller can write testimonials and design badges. Look for outside records and the exact terms.

steps.prompt: A moderator says the last seat needs a deposit by transfer tonight. What is your best reply?

choices.text: Send a small deposit so you do not lose the seat.
choices.consequence: A small transfer can lead to bigger demands, and it may be hard to get back.
choices.explanation: The size of the first ask authenticates neither the seller nor the account the money goes to.

choices.text: Let the deadline go until the recipient and the rules have been independently confirmed.
choices.consequence: The seat may be gone, but scarcity has not chosen your payment channel for you.
choices.explanation: A genuine organiser can explain the ordinary way to book. If they cannot, let the offer pass.

blocks.debrief: The free template, the public thank-you, the glowing quotes and the vanishing seat made a ladder, and every rung sat only a short reach above the last. On a replay, stop at the first rung where gratitude turns into an endorsement or a payment. What needs checking is the new stake. Nobody is asking you to distrust every friendly act.

questions.prompt: A colleague you trust gives you some free advice, then asks you to approve a new bank recipient. What matters most here?

choices.text: The change of recipient must go through the normal, independent approval route.
choices.explanation: Yes. Being grateful for the advice does not verify the bank details.

choices.text: The colleague has been generous, so the recipient must be safe.
choices.explanation: Reciprocity describes how you feel, not whether the bank details are sound.

questions.prompt: A real theatre has three tickets left at its own checkout. Does scarcity prove fraud?

choices.text: No. Make sure you are on the theatre’s long-established checkout, then decide freely.
choices.explanation: Right: stock may truly be low, but the payment route still matters.

choices.text: Yes. Every limited offer is a scam.
choices.explanation: A single cue cannot classify an offer.

questions.prompt: A page shows hundreds of glowing reviews for an investment app you have never heard of. What is the best inference?

choices.text: The reviews show that other people made money.
choices.explanation: Reviews can be fake or cherry-picked, and they cannot prove returns.

choices.text: The reviews are a reason to do some research, not proof that the app is safe.
choices.explanation: Right: check the company and the product through independent sources that bear on the claim.
